questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the first syllable of jiàoshòu mean?
How does the tone on jiào differ from the verb "to teach"?
What is Táidà an abbreviation for?
What is dropped from the second part of the sentence?
How do the Chinese characterize a person just identified?
Which earlier pattern does this resemble?

answers.answer_text: Wángfǔjǐng Dàjiē yǒu yíge Xīnhuá Shūdiàn, hěn dà.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "His wife is Japanese; she is in Shànghǎi now."

answers.answer_text: Tā tàitai shi Rìběn rén, xiànzài zài Shànghǎi.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Is the run-on structure acceptable in Chinese?

answers.answer_text: Yes — in Chinese this is a perfectly good way to add a second clause to a sentence.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "This is Professor Hollins, who teaches economics at Taiwan University."

answers.answer_text: Zhèiwèi shi Hé Jiàoshòu, zài Táidà jiāo jīngjìxué.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which counter is used for people in a polite introduction?

articles.text:
4. A: Zhèiwèi shi Hé Jiàoshòu, zài   This is Professor Hollins, who
      Táidà jiāo jīngjìxué.           teaches economics at Taiwan
                                       University.
   A: Hé Jiàoshòu, zhèiwèi shi       Professor Hollins, this is Section
      Huáng Kēzhǎng, zài Táiwān       Chief Huáng, who works at the
      Yínháng gōngzuò.                Bank of Taiwan.
   A: Zhèiwèi shi Huáng Tàitai.      This is Mrs. Huáng.

Notes on No. 4

Jiàoshòu, "professor": The first syllable in this word means "teaching." Notice that the tone on jiào is different from the tone on the verb "to teach," jiāo.

Táidà is the abbreviation for Táiwān Dàxué, "Taiwan University."

Zhèiwèi shi Huáng Kēzhǎng, zài Táiwān Yínháng gōngzuò looks like a run-on sentence, with the pronoun tā dropped from the second part of the sentence. In Chinese, this is a perfectly good way to add a second clause to a sentence. To characterize a person or thing just identified, the Chinese simply attach a descriptive sentence and omit the subject. You have already learned this pattern: Wángfǔjǐng Dàjiē yǒu yíge Xīnhuá Shūdiàn, hěn dà.

Tā tàitai shi Rìběn rén,         His wife is Japanese; she is in
xiànzài zài Shànghǎi.            Shànghǎi now.
Wǒ yǒu yíge péngyou xìng Wú,     I have a friend named Wú who teaches
zài Dōnghǎi Dàxué jiāo shū,      at Dōnghǎi University. He is
míngnián xiǎng dào Měiguo qù.    planning to go to America next year.
